_about: Published lived-experience research gathered for Waypoint Ledger (/lived-experience). Every quote is verbatim from the saved text in data/lived-experience-text/<id>.txt, whose sha256 is recorded here; tests/lived-experience.test.ts re-checks each one. These are published reports, studies and public testimony. None of it is an interview by us, and no composite built from it is a real person.

sources.title: Health+ Long COVID Human-Centered Design Report
sources.publisher: Coforma for the U.S. Department of Health and Human Services, Office of the Assistant Secretary for Health (Health+ program)

findings.finding: People with long COVID describe a loop of specialist visits; tests often come back normal and lead to yet another referral.
findings.quote: Normal results often lead to recommendations to see other specialists

findings.finding: One participant went to urgent care, a pulmonologist and a cardiologist; the X-ray and EKG were read as normal.
findings.quote: ‘X-Ray is clear. There’s nothing wrong with you.’ ‘Your EKG is fine. There’s nothing wrong with you.’

findings.finding: Symptoms are often put down to anxiety; one participant was asked about drugs and then given an anxiety diagnosis.
findings.quote: So, he also diagnosed me with anxiety.

findings.finding: People with long COVID can wait months, even a year, for a specialist appointment.
findings.quote: A person may spend months, or even a year, waiting for a specialist appointment.

findings.finding: A participant paid about $19,000 out of pocket in one year, mostly for a clinic insurance did not cover.
findings.quote: I paid about $19,000 out of pocket for medical bills the entire year.

findings.finding: Without insurance, people skip the hospital and the specialist they were told to see.
findings.quote: I didn’t want to go to the hospital because I didn’t have insurance.

findings.finding: Care usually starts with a primary care visit, urgent care or the emergency room.
findings.quote: they likely start by making an appointment with their primary care provider, visiting an urgent care center, or going to the emergency room.

findings.finding: One participant saw a pulmonologist and a cardiologist several times.
findings.quote: I went to a pulmonologist and a cardiologist a number of times.

findings.finding: Some are eventually referred to a long COVID clinic.
findings.quote: may be referred to a Long COVID clinic.

sources.title: Health+ Lyme Disease Human-Centered Design Report
sources.publisher: Coforma for the U.S. Department of Health and Human Services LymeX partnership (Health+ program)

findings.finding: One patient quoted in the report took seven and a half years to reach a diagnosis.
findings.quote: So seven-and-a-half years to get to diagnosis.

findings.finding: Patients describe years of doctor visits with every test negative and symptoms put down to stress.
findings.quote: I was just in and out of doctors for years and all my tests always came back negative

findings.finding: Symptoms were attributed to depression, anxiety or stress before Lyme was found.
findings.quote: a lot of my symptoms were pawned off to depression or anxiety or stress.

findings.finding: The report’s journey maps mark the point where insurance stops paying and costs build up.
findings.quote: Insurance usually drops off at this point, and medical costs start to build up

findings.finding: After a panel of negative tests, the primary care doctor refers on to a neurologist.
findings.quote: he didn't know what was wrong. So he's like, 'Oh, you need to go see a neurologist.'

findings.finding: In the HHS report’s own composite persona, negative tests led to a psychiatric evaluation.
findings.quote: The doctor then ordered a psychiatric evaluation on Mia that resulted in no answers.

findings.finding: In another HHS persona, the Lyme-literate doctor was paid out of pocket.
findings.quote: Sam was forced to pay out of pocket with the little money he had left to see an LLMD

sources.title: Health+ Sickle Cell Disease Human-Centered Design Report
sources.publisher: Coforma for the U.S. Department of Health and Human Services (Health+ program)

findings.finding: People with sickle cell disease describe the ER as a last resort, with long waits and accusations of drug seeking.
findings.quote: accusations of “drug seeking”, extended emergency department wait times, and difficulty filling prescriptions.

findings.finding: Adult ERs are busy and often unfamiliar with sickle cell protocols.
findings.quote: Adult ERs are busy, with long wait times

findings.finding: Gaps in primary care push people toward the ER and hospital, which is costly and traumatic.
findings.quote: The disconnect of primary care can result in increased ER visits and hospitalizations

findings.finding: A patient said they need a hematologist who knows sickle cell.
findings.quote: So that’s why I feel that I really need a hematologist down here.

findings.finding: In the ER, labs are run before pain is treated.
findings.quote: They have to run labs and they have to get the results of the labs

sources.title: Beyond Myalgic Encephalomyelitis/Chronic Fatigue Syndrome: Redefining an Illness (Summary)

findings.finding: Most ME/CFS patients surveyed waited more than a year for a diagnosis; most people with ME/CFS have never been diagnosed.
findings.quote: In multiple surveys, 67 to 77 percent of patients have reported that it took longer than 1 year to get a diagnosis

findings.finding: An estimated 84 to 91 percent of people with ME/CFS are not yet diagnosed.
findings.quote: an estimated 84 to 91 percent of patients affected by ME/CFS are not yet diagnosed

findings.finding: At least a quarter are house- or bedbound at some point; medical costs and lost earnings wreck household finances.
findings.quote: High medical costs combined with reduced earning capacity often have devastating effects on patients’ financial status.

sources.title: Toward a Common Research Agenda in Infection-Associated Chronic Illnesses: Proceedings of a Workshop (Chapter 2)
sources.publisher: National Academies of Sciences, Engineering, and Medicine (National Academies Press)

findings.finding: A speaker at the National Academies workshop said people are dismissed by their doctors every day.
findings.quote: every day people are going in to see their doctors and being dismissed.
findings.locator: 2 Overview of Infection-Associated Chronic Illnesses, page 16

findings.finding: Speakers asked that people living with these illnesses have their lived experiences supported.
findings.quote: those living with these challenges should have their lived experiences supported.
findings.locator: 2 Overview of Infection-Associated Chronic Illnesses, page 16

sources.title: A Long COVID Definition: A Chronic, Systemic Disease State with Profound Consequences (Summary)
sources.publisher: National Academies of Sciences, Engineering, and Medicine (National Academies Press)

findings.finding: Long COVID is diagnosed on clinical grounds; no available biomarker proves it.
findings.quote: No biomarker currently available demonstrates conclusively the presence of LC.

findings.finding: Long COVID can take away work, school, family care and self-care.
findings.quote: LC can impair individuals’ ability to work, attend school, take care of family, and care for themselves.

sources.title: Addressing Sickle Cell Disease: A Strategic Plan and Blueprint for Action (Chapter 5, Health Care Organization and Use)
sources.publisher: National Academies of Sciences, Engineering, and Medicine (National Academies Press)

findings.finding: Adults with sickle cell disease mostly get acute pain care in the emergency department.
findings.quote: Adults with SCD tend to seek acute care, primarily for pain, in the emergency department.
findings.locator: 5 Health Care Organization and Use, page 185

findings.finding: Guidelines say pain medicine within 30 minutes of triage, but timely re-dosing is rare in most EDs.
findings.quote: it is rare in most EDs, for variety of reasons.
findings.locator: 5 Health Care Organization and Use, page 213

sources.title: Charting a Path Toward New Treatments for Lyme Infection-Associated Chronic Illnesses (Chapter 1, Introduction)
sources.publisher: National Academies of Sciences, Engineering, and Medicine (National Academies Press)

findings.finding: Up to half of the illness costs of persistent Lyme symptoms are paid out of pocket, often for therapies insurance does not cover.
findings.quote: Up to half of the illness-related costs are borne out-of-pocket

findings.finding: Without a diagnostic test, people with persistent Lyme symptoms are stigmatized and dismissed.
findings.quote: have often led to stigmatization and dismissal of people living with Lyme IACI by the health care system

sources.title: Sickle Cell Disease in Social Security Disability Evaluations: Pain and Treatment Settings (Chapter 4, Health Care Delivery)
sources.publisher: National Academies of Sciences, Engineering, and Medicine (National Academies Press)

findings.finding: An adult with sickle cell disease told the committee a crisis now means five to six days in hospital.
findings.quote: My hospitalizations used to be 3 days tops. Now I’m in the hospital 5 to 6 days.
findings.locator: 4 Health Care Delivery in Sickle Cell Disease, page 89

findings.finding: The same person has one to two crises a year and must go to the emergency department for each.
findings.quote: I experience one to two crises annually.
findings.locator: 4 Health Care Delivery in Sickle Cell Disease, page 89

findings.finding: Pain medicine came in 62 minutes at an infusion center against 132 minutes in the emergency department.
findings.quote: time to administer pain medication at an infusion center was 62 minutes compared to 132 minutes in the emergency department
findings.locator: 4 Health Care Delivery in Sickle Cell Disease, page 85

sources.title: Characterizing long COVID in an international cohort: 7 months of symptoms and their impact

findings.finding: For more than 91 percent of 3,762 respondents, recovery took longer than 35 weeks.
findings.quote: For the majority of respondents (>91%), the time to recovery exceeded 35 weeks.

findings.finding: 45.2 percent needed a reduced work schedule and 22.3 percent were not working because of their health.
findings.quote: 45.2% (42.9% to 47.2%) of respondents reported requiring a reduced work schedule compared to pre-illness.

sources.title: The face of postural tachycardia syndrome - insights from a large cross-sectional online community-based survey
sources.where: United States and other countries (online survey)

findings.finding: People with POTS saw a median of five physicians before diagnosis; 21 percent saw more than ten.
findings.quote: On average, patients saw 7 ± 11 [median 5 (IQR 3–8)] physicians prior to a diagnosis of POTS.
findings.locator: Section: Diagnostic journey travelled by POTS patients

findings.finding: 77 percent were told by a physician their symptoms were psychiatric or psychological.
findings.quote: There were 3471 (77%) respondents who encountered a physician who suggested their symptoms were due to a psychiatric or psychological problem

findings.finding: The median wait from first visit to diagnosis was 24 months; the mean was 4.9 years.
findings.quote: Respondents waited a median time of 24 (IQR 6–72) months (4.9 ± 7.1 years) after initial presentation to a physician
findings.locator: Section: Diagnostic journey travelled by POTS patients

findings.finding: Respondents averaged nine emergency department visits before diagnosis.
findings.quote: Number of ED visits prior to diagnosis 9 (16)
findings.locator: Section: Diagnostic journey travelled by POTS patients

sources.title: Severity of chronic Lyme disease compared to other chronic conditions: a quality of life survey

findings.finding: 61.7 percent of respondents with persistent Lyme symptoms were not diagnosed for at least two years.
findings.quote: 61.7% were not diagnosed for at least 2 years.
findings.locator: Section: Study inclusion and exclusion criteria.

findings.finding: They reported more health care use and greater out-of-pocket medical costs than people with other chronic diseases.
findings.quote: increased utilization of healthcare services, and greater out of pocket medical costs.

sources.title: Obstacles to diagnosis and treatment of Lyme disease in the USA: a qualitative study

findings.finding: Ten of 26 patients went first to urgent care or the ER, where misdiagnosis was more common.
findings.quote: Misdiagnoses were more common in these settings, contributing to treatment delay.

findings.finding: One patient was told in the ER it was bursitis or tendonitis.
findings.quote: I went up to the ER and they told me I had bursitis.

findings.finding: Lacking insurance delayed people from seeing a doctor at all.
findings.quote: I didn’t have insurance. That was one of the main things.

findings.finding: Half first went to a primary care provider; 38.5 percent first went to urgent care or the ER.
findings.quote: Half of the participants first sought care for Lyme disease from a primary care provider

sources.title: The Journey of Adult Patients with Lyme Disease in the United States: A Qualitative Interview Study and Patient-Reported, Health-Related Quality-of-Life Assessment

findings.finding: Adults with Lyme disease reported fear, anxiety, needing time off work and more time indoors at diagnosis.
findings.quote: Participants reported various impacts at diagnosis, such as fear and anxiety, difficulty exercising, needing time off work, and spending increased time indoors.

findings.finding: Most had a Lyme ELISA blood test.
findings.quote: Most participants (20/25, 80%) documented having an LD enzyme-linked immunosorbent assay (ELISA) test

findings.finding: Most were referred on to an infectious disease doctor after the first visit.
findings.quote: participants frequently reported being referred to an infectious disease doctor after their initial healthcare provider visit.

sources.title: Comorbidity, misdiagnoses, and the diagnostic odyssey in patients with hypermobile Ehlers-Danlos syndrome

findings.finding: People with hypermobile EDS saw an average of 15.6 clinicians and waited 10.39 years for the diagnosis.
findings.quote: respondents saw an average of 15.6 clinicians (24% reported that they saw 20 or more), and the average time to diagnosis was 10.39 years

findings.finding: Anxiety and depression were the most common alternative diagnoses given before hEDS.
findings.quote: Anxiety, depression, and migraines were the most common.

findings.finding: Most received the diagnosis from a genetics specialist, then a rheumatologist.
findings.quote: The majority (57%) received their official diagnosis of hEDS from a genetics specialist

findings.finding: After genetics, the next most common diagnosing clinicians were rheumatologists and primary care physicians.
findings.quote: followed by a rheumatologist (20%) or their primary care physician (5%).

sources.title: Defining the Chronic Complexities of hEDS and HSD: A Global Survey of Diagnostic Challenges, Life-Long Comorbidities, and Unmet Needs

findings.finding: Survey respondents with hEDS reported an average diagnostic delay of 22.1 years.
findings.quote: Participants with hEDS reported a mean of 24 comorbid conditions and an average diagnostic delay of 22.1 years.

findings.finding: 31.3 percent of hEDS respondents travelled 300 miles or more for care.
findings.quote: 31.3% of hEDS and 9.5% of HSD participants report having traveled 300 or more miles

findings.finding: Many paid out of pocket for a specialist not covered by insurance.
findings.quote: many participants report paying out-of-pocket for medical care from a specialist not covered by insurance.

findings.finding: The specialties they visit most are family medicine, cardiology, gastroenterology, neurology and emergency medicine.
findings.quote: The most frequently visited specialties included family medicine, cardiology, gastroenterology, neurology/neurosurgery, and emergency medicine.

sources.title: Sources and consequences of self-doubt in patients with Ehlers-Danlos syndrome: a qualitative study in Europe and North America

findings.finding: Repeated dismissal in health care, especially in childhood, left people with EDS doubting their own pain.
findings.quote: Participants attributed much of their self-doubt to repeated dismissal and minimisation of their symptoms in healthcare settings, especially during childhood.

findings.finding: Some withdrew from conventional medicine altogether.
findings.quote: others withdrew from the conventional medical system altogether.

sources.title: A qualitative study of pain and related symptoms experienced by people with Ehlers-Danlos syndromes

findings.finding: Few relied on the health care system; most built their own strategies, including complementary care.
findings.quote: Very few relied on a “system” of health care and instead developed their own strategies

sources.title: Medically explained symptoms: a mixed methods study of diagnostic, symptom and support experiences of patients with lupus and related systemic autoimmune diseases

findings.finding: Mean time from first symptoms to a lupus or related diagnosis was 6 years 11 months.
findings.quote: The mean time to diagnosis from first experiencing symptoms was 6 years 11 months.

findings.finding: 76 percent had at least one misdiagnosis; mental health misdiagnoses were 47 percent of them.
findings.quote: Seventy-six per cent reported at least one misdiagnosis

findings.finding: One respondent was sent to a psychiatrist because blood results were normal; the psychiatrist sent her back to a new rheumatologist.
findings.quote: The rheumatologist sent me to see a psychiatrist because I complained that I felt ill even though the blood results were OK.

findings.finding: Clinicians seen included the GP, rheumatologist, lupus specialist, A&E doctor, neurologist and others.
findings.quote: GP, rheumatologist, lupus specialist, accident and emergency (A&E) doctor, specialist nurse, physiotherapist, neurologist
findings.locator: Section: Clinician support: knowledge, trust and listening skills

findings.finding: People whose ANA blood test stayed negative waited 13 years on average.
findings.quote: mean delay of 13 years for permanently ANA-negative participants

findings.finding: The psychiatrist sent the same respondent back to find a new rheumatologist.
findings.quote: I should get a new rheumatologist who knew more about lupus

sources.title: Diagnostic overshadowing in systemic lupus erythematosus (SLE): A qualitative study

findings.finding: GPs put symptoms down to anxiety, stress or "nothing wrong" for years.
findings.quote: GP said: ‘Maybe there’s an element of anxiety there’.

findings.finding: Some clinicians stopped investigating because it was too expensive to continue.
findings.quote: particularly when the clinician indicated that it was too expensive to keep investigating.

sources.title: Investigating the ME/CFS experience through qualitative analysis of memorial entries
sources.where: United States (National CFIDS Foundation memorial list)

findings.finding: Published memorial records describe misdiagnosis, dismissal and unhelpful treatment recommendations.
findings.quote: Negative healthcare experiences included misdiagnosis and misattribution of symptoms, dismissal, inadequate knowledge and experience with treating ME/CFS, and the recommendation of unhelpful treatments.

sources.title: Understanding symptom clusters, diagnosis and healthcare experiences in myalgic encephalomyelitis/chronic fatigue syndrome and long COVID: a cross-sectional survey in the UK

findings.finding: Time to an ME/CFS diagnosis ranged widely: 22.1 percent in one to two years, 12.9 percent more than ten.
findings.quote: with 22.1% diagnosed within 1–2 years of symptom onset and 12.9% taking more than 10 years.

sources.title: Under-Served Groups and Myalgic Encephalomyelitis Research Workshop; Multiple Barriers to Effective Healthcare, Research and Public Participation

findings.finding: People with ME from under-served groups face barriers to care twice over.
findings.quote: who appear doubly disadvantaged by their illness and their socioeconomic and/or ethnic background.

sources.title: Attitudes and Beliefs Regarding Pain and Discrimination Among Black Adults with Sickle Cell Disease: A Mixed Methods Evaluation of an Adapted Chronic Pain Intervention

findings.finding: Adults with sickle cell disease describe being treated as drug-seeking when they ask for pain relief.
findings.quote: they’re looking at you like you’re, you’re a drug addict trying to, and you’re just in pain

findings.finding: Most described racism or discrimination in medical settings and clinicians’ lack of knowledge.
findings.quote: Most described at least one experience of racism or discrimination in the medical setting

sources.title: The Impact of Long COVID on Employment and Well-Being: A Qualitative Study of Patient Perspectives

findings.finding: Working through long COVID left little energy, even for recommended appointments.
findings.quote: made it difficult to attend recommended healthcare appointments.

findings.finding: Loss of income and changes in insurance were compounded by high health care costs.
findings.quote: loss of income and changes in insurance, which were compounded by high healthcare costs.

sources.title: Long COVID and financial hardship: A disaggregated analysis at income and education levels

findings.finding: In federal BRFSS data, lost or reduced work hours explained 6 to 20 percent of long COVID financial hardship.
findings.quote: lost or reduced hours of employment accounted for a significant portion (6%–20%) of the changes in financial distress.

sources.title: Barriers to healthcare access and experiences of stigma: Findings from a coproduced Long Covid case-finding study

findings.finding: Self-doubt, sometimes reinforced by clinicians, kept people from seeking care.
findings.quote: There was considerable self‐doubt among participants, sometimes reinforced by interactions with healthcare professionals (HCPs).

sources.title: Characterization of Postural Orthostatic Tachycardia Syndrome in Long COVID: Self-reported Data From the LISTEN Study

findings.finding: People with long COVID who developed POTS reported more financial difficulty and isolation.
findings.quote: Participants with self-reported POTS were younger, had more financial difficulties, more social isolation

sources.title: A qualitative exploration of illness-related experiences, emotions, and coping among adults with postural orthostatic tachycardia syndrome (POTS)

findings.finding: One participant avoided a tilt-table test for fear a negative result would mean being told nothing was wrong.
findings.quote: I was worried that if it wasn’t then I would be treated like, ‘Oh, there is nothing.’

sources.title: One or many labels? a longitudinal qualitative study of patients' journey to diagnosis at a specialist NHS Postural Tachycardia Syndrome (PoTS) clinic

findings.finding: Waiting for a POTS clinic, people go through tilt-table tests and repeated blood tests.
findings.quote: every time they do blood tests, basically, they’re finding more problems, so it just feels relentless
findings.locator: Section: The value and impact of investigations

findings.finding: Referral to the specialist POTS clinic follows symptoms and/or a suggestive tilt-table test.
findings.quote: suggestive tilt-table test results.

sources.title: The Diagnostic Journey of Dysautonomia Patients: Insights from a Patient-Reported Outcome Study

findings.finding: People with dysautonomia waited 7.7 years on average; cardiologists and neurologists made most diagnoses.
findings.quote: The average time to diagnosis was 7.7 years (SD 10 years) and diagnosis was made primarily by cardiologists, followed by neurologists

findings.finding: Diagnoses came from cardiologists, then neurologists, then internists or primary care physicians.
findings.quote: diagnosis was made primarily by cardiologists, followed by neurologists, and internists or primary care physicians.

sources.title: Testimony of Nicole Heim, parent of a teenager with long COVID, Senate HELP hearing “Addressing Long COVID: Advancing Research and Improving Patient Care”
sources.publisher: U.S. Senate Committee on Health, Education, Labor, and Pensions

findings.finding: A parent waited many months, through Medicaid prior authorization, for a pediatric long COVID clinic.
findings.quote: After many months of waiting and jumping through prior authorization hoops with Medicaid

findings.finding: Her daughter, sick since age 14, is now homeschooled full-time.
findings.quote: is now homeschooled full-time.

findings.finding: While waiting for the clinic, testing and blood work continued.
findings.quote: my daughter’s testing and blood work continued.

sources.title: Testimony of Angela Meriquez Vazquez, Senate HELP hearing “Addressing Long COVID: Advancing Research and Improving Patient Care”
sources.publisher: U.S. Senate Committee on Health, Education, Labor, and Pensions

findings.finding: Abnormal labs within weeks of infection were dismissed as anxiety.
findings.quote: All were dismissed by doctors as anxiety

sources.title: Testimony of Rachel Beale, Senate HELP hearing “Addressing Long COVID: Advancing Research and Improving Patient Care”
sources.publisher: U.S. Senate Committee on Health, Education, Labor, and Pensions

findings.finding: A human resources director moved to long-term disability and lost her job.
findings.quote: There is nothing that prepares you to hear the words that you no longer have a job.

findings.finding: Her disability insurance application was denied twice.
findings.quote: I have been denied twice.

findings.finding: Even with good insurance, the copays add up.
findings.quote: However, the copays add up. Sometimes we can’t pay for them on time.

findings.finding: She has been sick for almost three years.
findings.quote: I’ve been sick for almost three years.
